A Bad Deal on Calories

Source: Cole (2017), Scientific Reports
Talking in class:
Miya
Deer muscle163,000five times human muscle (about 32,000)
Woolly rhinoceros1.26 millioncalories offered
Woolly mammoth3.6 millioncalories offered
A big animal beat a person as a meal
Across human history, most societies
have shared one rule:
you do not eat other people.
We usually treat it as a moral boundary.
But some scientists argue that
biology may have helped build it.
Today we follow the evidence,
from a mysterious disease in Papua
New Guinea to the calories inside
a human body.
Our story begins in the 1950s,
in the eastern highlands of Papua New Guinea.
The Fore people lived there,
largely cut off from the outside world.
When researchers arrived, they
found a disease that kept killing people.
Victims began to tremble,
lost their balance, and slowly
lost control of their bodies.
The Fore called it kuru,
a word that means trembling.
Outsiders sometimes called it the
laughing sickness, because patients
could burst into sudden,
uncontrolled laughter.
After the first symptoms,
most patients died within about a year.
By the end, they could no longer
walk or swallow.
In total, kuru killed roughly 2,700 people.
Doctors were baffled.
Kuru did not behave like flu,
cholera, or malaria.
Patients had no fever,
and there was no sign of the
usual inflammation.
It also struck unevenly.
At its peak, kuru was eight to
nine times more common among women
and children than among men.
The answer lay in how the Fore mourned.
When a relative died,
the family did not bury the body.
Instead, they ate it,
as an act of grief and respect.
Anthropologists call this mortuary
cannibalism.
For the Fore, it was a way
of caring for the dead.
The body was shared by custom.
Men usually ate the muscle.
Women and children usually ate
the brain and other organs.
That detail matters, because the
brain is where the infectious agent
was most concentrated.
A ritual of love had become a
path for a deadly infection.
Under the microscope, the brains
of kuru victims looked full of
holes, like a sponge.
Nerve cells had died,
leaving empty spaces in the tissue.
This pattern gives the whole family
of diseases its name:
transmissible spongiform encephalopathy,
which means a contagious,
sponge-like brain disease.
For decades, scientists believed
every infection needed genetic
material, DNA or RNA,
to copy itself.
Kuru broke that rule.
The agent was unusually hard to
destroy with heat, radiation,
and disinfectants.
In 1982, neurologist Stanley Prusiner
proposed an infectious particle
made of protein alone.
He named it the prion.
Proteins work only when they fold
into the right shape.
A healthy brain makes a normal
prion protein, called PrP-C.
A misfolded version, called PrP-Sc,
has a different shape.
When it meets a normal copy,
it can push that copy into the
same wrong shape.
It spreads without dividing,
like a molecular zombie.
That starts a slow chain reaction.
One misfolded protein converts
another, which converts more.
The misfolded proteins clump together,
and the nerve cells around them die.
The body has no good way to
clear them away, so the damage
keeps adding up until the brain
can no longer work.
You might ask: could you just cook the meat?
Unfortunately, no.
Ordinary germs like Salmonella
are killed by normal cooking heat.
Prions are far tougher.
They can survive standard sterilization,
and in lab studies some infectivity
remained even after heating to
600 degrees Celsius.
Formalin does not reliably destroy
them either.
Your immune system does not help much either.
A prion is made from a protein
your own body makes,
just folded wrongly, so it does
not look foreign.
Researchers see no antibody response
and no inflammation in these diseases.
The infection can travel quietly
toward the brain without setting
off any alarm.
Then there is the waiting.
Many infections show up within days.
Kuru could stay silent for years,
and in some cases for more than fifty years.
Someone could be exposed as a child,
feel perfectly healthy for decades,
and still fall ill much later.
Once symptoms begin, kuru has been fatal.
The world saw a similar story in
the 1990s with mad cow disease.
Cattle were fed meat-and-bone meal
made from the remains of other cattle.
The result was bovine spongiform
encephalopathy, and it later passed
to people as variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob
disease.
Feeding an animal its own species
turned out to be a dangerous experiment.
Now to a different question.
Did people ever eat each other
simply for food?
Archaeologist James Cole, at the
University of Brighton, decided
to count the calories.
His 2017 study, published in Scientific
Reports, used body composition
data to estimate how much energy
a human body actually contains.
The numbers are modest.
An adult man holds roughly 126,000
calories in total.
Only about 32,000 of those are
in the muscle, the part that works like meat.
The heart gives about 650 calories,
and the brain and spinal cord about 2,700.
Compare that with other prey.
Deer muscle holds about 163,000
calories, five times more than human muscle.
A woolly rhinoceros offers about
1.26 million, and a woolly mammoth
about 3.6 million.
For hunters, a large animal was
a far better meal than a person.
Hunting people was also dangerous.
Humans use tools, plan ahead,
and fight back.
A hunt for another person risks
injury and revenge, for a small
calorie reward.
This suggests that when people
did eat people, food may not have
been the main reason.
Biology adds another warning.
Some pollutants, such as mercury
and certain industrial chemicals,
build up as they move up the food chain.
Scientists call this biomagnification.
Humans eat high on the food chain,
so human tissue can carry these substances.
How much would depend on the person.
Germs from other humans are already
adapted to human bodies.
The species barrier protects us
from many animal germs,
because their biology differs from ours.
With human meat, that barrier is gone.
How much risk depends on the pathogen,
but the protection is missing.
Even our feelings may carry this lesson.
Disgust is not just a social habit.
Research links it to avoiding contamination
and disease, and brain imaging
studies connect it to a region
called the insula.
It is a fast,
automatic signal that helps keep
us away from things that could
make us sick.
Here is a thought experiment,
not a proven history.
Imagine two ancient groups.
In one, people tolerate eating their dead.
In the other, people feel strong
disgust at it.
If prion disease spread in the
first group, it would suffer more.
Over many generations, avoidance
could be favored by natural selection.
Some genetic evidence points the same way.
In 2003, researchers studied the
prion protein gene, called PRNP.
People who carry two different
versions at position 129 are more
resistant to prion disease.
The pattern of these versions around
the world is consistent with ancient
kuru-like epidemics.
In Papua New Guinea,
the epidemic ended once the practice stopped.
After an Australian administration
ban, the Fore largely stopped eating
the dead around 1960.
Because of the long incubation
period, people kept falling ill for decades.
The last known death from kuru
was in 2009.
The lessons reached modern hospitals.
Because prions resist ordinary
sterilization, health agencies
set special rules for instruments
used on high-risk tissue,
including stronger chemical treatments
and longer high-temperature cycles.
In the past, prion disease has
also spread through some medical
routes, which is why those rules exist.
So what does this add up to?
Cannibalism carries real biological
risks: prion disease, no species
barrier, and a poor calorie return.
These facts do not explain every
taboo, and cultures differ.
But they suggest that the rule
against eating people may rest
on more than morality alone.
Next time you hear about cannibalism
in a legend or a horror film,
remember the quieter horror.
It lives in a protein that folds
the wrong way, in a disease that
waits for decades, and in a ledger
of calories that never added up.
The evidence suggests our ancestors
had good reasons to say:
do not eat another person.
